title: Sharing the Burden: A Feasible Path to Land Value Taxation
what_was_fetched: SSRN abstract page fully blocked by Cloudflare under every method tried: direct curl with browser UA (403, JS challenge page), r.jina.ai proxy (blocked, 'Just a moment...'/CAPTCHA notice), curl with Googlebot UA (403 'Content Blocked' — SSRN/Elsevier's own bot-block page, not a Cloudflare challenge, so the Googlebot trick that works on Springer does not work here), WebFetch (403 Forbidden), the alternate ssrn.com/abstract= domain (same Cloudflare block), the Delivery.cfm direct-PDF URL pattern (403), and Wayback Machine (no snapshot archived yet — paper is 8 days old as of today). No PDF was obtained. RECOVERED the abstract text and full metadata via a different route: Crossref's public API for the paper's own DOI (10.2139/ssrn.7442118), which SSRN deposits automatically on posting — this returned the verbatim abstract, both authors' ORCIDs, and the paper's own reference list (3 works cited). WebSearch could not locate any mirror (author site, working-paper repository, ResearchGate) — the paper appears genuinely not yet indexed anywhere outside SSRN/Crossref.
verdict: ENRICH objections/lvt-transition-wealth-shock (primary) and objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor (secondary) — but only once a T1 obtains the full text; the Crossref abstract alone is enough to know the mechanism and confirm it is new, not enough to draft from since the working mechanics of the proportional-allocation rule are not stated beyond one sentence.
claim_grade: B — abstract-level only, but the abstract text itself is machine-verified against the metadata SSRN submitted to Crossref (not a paraphrase, snippet, or secondary report), so it is as reliable as an abstract gets. NOT A: no full text, methodology, or worked example was read. A T1 or a future T0 pass MUST get the PDF (try: SSRN via an authenticated institutional proxy if T1 has one; check back in ~2-4 weeks for a Wayback snapshot; email/contact Tideman directly — he has historically shared working papers; check the Virginia Tech econ department's working paper series; check Jacobson's Uppsala DiVA portal, which already hosts his PhD thesis at uu.diva-portal.org and may pick this up as a co-authored working paper).
mechanism_found: Full Crossref-deposited abstract (verbatim): "A practice of regarding a mortgage as a taxable interest in land when the mortgage exceeds the value of the improvements to the land and of allocating an increase in land taxes between title holders and mortgage holders in proportion to their interests can guarantee that title holders will not go 'underwater' (have negative equity) when land taxes are increased." This is a specific, novel transition-design proposal: when a mortgage's balance exceeds the value of the building/improvements on the parcel (i.e., the lender's effective collateral interest extends into the land value, not just the structure), the mortgage itself is treated as carrying a taxable interest in the land. Any land-tax increase during a transition to LVT is then split between the titleholder (homeowner) and the mortgage holder (lender) IN PROPORTION TO THEIR RESPECTIVE INTERESTS — the guarantee being that this proportional allocation mathematically prevents the titleholder's equity from going negative as the tax rises. This is a lender-cost-sharing mechanism, not a deferral, phase-in-speed, or exemption mechanism.
authors_confirmed: T. Nicolaus Tideman (ORCID 0000-0002-3971-5965) and Martin Jacobson (ORCID 0000-0002-5824-3844). Jacobson is confirmed via WebSearch as a political theorist at Uppsala University's Department of Government, who defended a June 2024 PhD thesis 'Land & Liberty: On the Natural Monopoly of Violence' on the geoism/left-libertarian-anarchism relationship (hosted at uu.diva-portal.org) — a genuine Georgist scholar, not a name coincidence. He presented 'Economic Democracy: A Left-Libertarian Perspective' at the 2026 Public Choice Society conference in the same organized session where Tideman presented. No existing wiki page for Jacobson.
paper_references_confirm_framing: The paper's own 3-item reference list (from Crossref) is: Laurence J. Kotlikoff, 'Jimmy Stewart Is Dead: Ending the World's Ongoing Financial Plague with Limited Purpose Banking' (2010); Mancur Olson, 'The Logic of Collective Action' (1971); Gordon Tullock, 'The Transitional Gains Trap,' Bell Journal of Economics 6(2):671 (1975). The Tullock citation is significant: it directly ties this paper to the exact theoretical frame objections/lvt-transition-wealth-shock.md already cites (via its 'public-choice critique' See Also link) as 'the theoretical parent of this objection.' The Kotlikoff limited-purpose-banking citation suggests the mortgage/lender-interest mechanism may be framed within a broader banking-reform argument (Kotlikoff's book proposes banks hold only equity-financed mutual funds, no leveraged deposit-taking) — worth checking once full text is available, since it could mean the mechanism assumes a banking-system redesign beyond ordinary mortgage law, which would be an important caveat for how 'feasible' the 'feasible path' actually is.
existing_wiki_coverage: objections/lvt-transition-wealth-shock.md (29 backlinks) already covers: phase-in speed (citing Common Wealth Canada's price-reaction model), the 'one-time transfer not ongoing cost' framing, pairing with cuts to other taxes (ATCOR), deferral/compensation for hardship cases (cross-linked to lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor), the full compensation-vs-no-compensation spectrum from Mill to George's own uncompensated position (Progress and Poverty Book VII Ch. III, quoted), the contested Danish capitalization evidence (DORS full-capitalization vs. Nielsson et al. zero-capitalization), and explicitly names Tullock's transitional-gains trap as 'the theoretical parent of this objection' via a See Also link to objections/public-choice-critique. It generically notes 'recent buyers and the highly leveraged are hit hardest' but has NO mechanism that specifically addresses mortgage holders' liability or negative equity — this is the clean, novel delta. objections/lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor.md (28 backlinks, not fully read this session but confirmed by title/tags to cover the 'little old lady in a valuable house' cash-flow objection) is the secondary target since a proportional lender/borrower split is also a way of avoiding a cash-poor owner having to find the money themselves. No existing wiki content anywhere mentions treating a mortgage as a taxable land interest, or splitting an LVT-transition tax increase between titleholder and lender.
uncertainties: 1. This is a ONE-SENTENCE abstract; I do not know the paper's worked mechanics — how the mortgage's 'interest in land' is quantified when it exceeds improvement value, how 'proportion of their interests' is calculated as land value (and hence the tax base) itself changes over the transition, what happens to lenders who did not agree to this reallocation ex ante (a retroactive reallocation of tax liability onto mortgage holders is a real legal/political lift), or whether the guarantee holds under a full transition to 100% LVT or only partial shifts. 2. I do not know if 'Sharing the Burden' in the title refers ONLY to this titleholder/lender split, or if the paper proposes additional burden-sharing devices (e.g., across government levels, or between land uses) not captured in the one-sentence abstract. 3. Tideman has substantial existing wiki coverage (people/nicolaus-tideman.md, 15 backlinks; research/tideman-avoidable-excess-burden; research/tideman-plassmann-land-assembly; research/tideman-plassmann-losses-of-nations; research/bentick-mills-timing-neutrality documents 'the Tideman rebuttal') — a T1 should check whether this 2026 paper cites or extends any of that prior work, which the abstract alone cannot show. 4. Do not draft a page from the abstract alone — the EDITORIAL acceptance rule for objection pages requires citing 'the strongest available version' of a response, and a one-sentence abstract is too thin to responsibly characterize a 'feasible path' claim without seeing how the authors themselves qualify or limit it.

title: Here's one way to protect Forsyth, Guilford homeowners from surging property taxes (Winston-Salem Journal, John Deem, published 2026-09-18)
what_was_fetched: Full article text obtained directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, no paywall hit) and independently cross-verified via the r.jina.ai reader proxy (also HTTP 200, clean markdown extraction) — both methods agree. This is a full-text, A-grade fetch.
verdict: ENRICH concepts/split-rate-taxation (terminology-note footnote only) — REJECT for any LVT-substantive page. This is the Massachusetts-style classification confusion, explicitly, not genuine land/building split-rate LVT.
claim_grade: A for what the article says (full text read, verbatim quotes below); but the underlying policy itself is speculative journalism about a hypothetical, not a real bill — there is nothing pending in the NC General Assembly to grade as a policy proposal. Grade the FACTS about NC's situation as A; grade the 'split-rate could fix this' idea as a floated hypothetical from one advocate, not a proposal with any legislative status.
is_it_genuine_lvt: No. Direct quote: 'Giving local governments the ability to set varying rates for RESIDENTIAL, COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL properties would allow them to control how much of the tax burden is borne by owners in each of the three categories.' This is a property-CLASS rate differential (the article even cites DC's system as a precedent: 'commercial and industrial properties taxed at about twice the rate of residential homes... vacant tracts are more than five times higher... blighted properties are taxed 10 times more' — again, all classification-based, not land-vs-improvement-based). There is no land/building value-split mechanism proposed anywhere in the article. The article does mention that 'a handful of cities in Virginia and Pennsylvania use split-rate systems' in the same breath as the DC classification example, without distinguishing that PA's system IS genuine land/building split-rate while DC's is classification-based — the article itself conflates the two meanings, which is exactly the confusion the wiki's existing terminology note exists to prevent.
who_is_proposing_it_and_at_what_stage: Nobody has introduced a bill. The idea is floated as a hypothetical by Theo Nollert (policy director, Carolina Forward — a NC progressive nonprofit — and a Chapel Hill Town Council member), in response to the reporter's question about ways to cushion homeowners after reassessment shocks. Direct quote from Nollert: 'If you create local authority to tax in that way, then all of a sudden you've created a new tool for local governments to decide what they want to incentivize.' The article frames this as one of several options being discussed (alongside a Nov. 2026 ballot constitutional amendment letting the General Assembly cap local rate increases, and legislative delays to Guilford County's 2026 reassessment) — not as a bill with a number, sponsor, or committee status.
legal_position_under_nc_law: Blocked. Direct quote from Chris McLaughlin (law professor, UNC School of Government): 'the state's existing property tax structure is protected by the North Carolina Constitution's Uniformity Clause and would require a constitutional amendment to alter.' McLaughlin is also quoted skeptical of political viability: 'I think owners of commercial properties would work hard to defeat any such proposed amendment.'
key_factual_content_if_used: Forsyth County's actual 2025 reassessment (the real-world trigger for this discussion, not hypothetical): countywide residential property values rose 60% vs. 40% for everything else; residential share of the county's total tax burden jumped from 59% to 64% (63%→68% in the city of Winston-Salem) overnight, purely from the value-mix shift, before any rate was even set. Median home value rose 72%, from $156,700 (2024) to $269,700 (2025) [Deputy Tax Assessor Michael Pollock, single completed dwellings only, excluding rural parcels]. Even after both city and county cut their nominal rates to near revenue-neutral, the county tax bill for a median-valued home rose 33% to $1,316/year and the city bill rose 41% to $1,394/year — a combined 34% increase to $2,710/year. The article's own hypothetical modelling: had a 'residential-neutral' rate held the residential value-share constant at the pre-reassessment 59%/63% shares instead of letting it float to 64%/68%, the median home's tax increase would have been 5.6% (county) and 12% (city) instead of the actual 22%/31% revenue-neutral-rate increases — illustrating how much of the 'tax shock' homeowners experienced was a pure mix-shift effect of residential values outpacing commercial, not a policy choice.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/split-rate-taxation.md (52 backlinks) already carries a precise, directly analogous precedent in its 'Terminology note': Delaware's 2026 HB 462, which lets New Castle County school districts tax commercial/apartment property up to 185% of the residential rate, is flagged there verbatim as 'the other, non-Georgist meaning: it is a class-based rate differential, not a land-value instrument, and has no bearing on this page.' No existing wiki page covers North Carolina, Forsyth County, Winston-Salem, or Guilford County at all (confirmed by repo grep — zero hits for 'north carolina' outside unrelated Gaffney archive texts and narrative pages about a different topic).
uncertainties: 1. Because nothing is actually proposed as a bill, I am uncertain this clears the bar for its own events/ page — it may be better as a single added sentence in the split-rate-taxation.md terminology note (following the Delaware HB 462 precedent format exactly), not a standalone entry. 2. If T1 wants broader NC property-tax-politics coverage (the Uniformity Clause, the Nov. 2026 rate-cap ballot amendment, the Guilford reassessment delay), that is a distinct, non-Georgist story about ordinary property-tax administration politics with no land-value angle at all — I would not recommend a full places/north-carolina.md page on the strength of this article alone. 3. I have not verified independently whether Virginia and Pennsylvania cities' split-rate systems (cited by the article as precedent) are genuinely land-value split-rate (as the wiki's Pennsylvania/Harrisburg/Pittsburgh pages already document) or whether the reporter is using 'split-rate' loosely there too — worth a footnote caveat if cited, since the article itself does not clearly distinguish.

title: Value-based property tax, no water or power: What Telangana's CURE law means for Hyderabad (NewsMeter, published 2026-09-12)
what_was_fetched: Full article text obtained via r.jina.ai reader proxy (HTTP 200, complete clean extraction covering the whole piece section-by-section); direct curl also succeeded (HTTP 200) as a redundant confirmation the page is not paywalled. Full-text A-grade fetch of this secondary news report. NOT fetched: the primary CURE 2026 Bill text itself (introduced in the Telangana Assembly; I did not locate or attempt to retrieve the bill document from a Telangana government source in this session).
verdict: NEW PAGE events/2026-telangana-cure-law-hyderabad (or research/, per T1's preferred convention for a single-jurisdiction legislative case study) — genuinely new, thin existing India coverage, and directly on-topic (a shift from rental-value to land-value property tax basis).
claim_grade: B — a single, detailed secondary news report with specific section numbers and figures (suggesting direct familiarity with the actual Bill text), but I did not independently verify against the primary Bill document or an official Telangana government source, and this is a Bill that had only just been introduced in the Assembly (not yet passed) as of the article's Sep 12 publication date.
what_actually_changed_and_valuation_basi: The CURE (Core Urban Region) 2026 Bill, introduced in the Telangana Assembly, proposes replacing the GHMC Act 1955 with a unified law for Hyderabad's Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, Malkajgiri Municipal Corporation and Cyberabad Municipal Corporation (within the Outer Ring Road). Direct quote on the tax-basis change: 'The existing annual rental value-based system would be replaced with a land-value-based system.' This is a genuine ARV-to-land-value shift, not a classification split and not a capital-value (land+building) system — the valuation basis is explicitly LAND value. Proposed rates: residential buildings 0.10%-0.50% of land value; non-residential buildings 0.20%-2% of land value; vacant plots 0.50% of land value (notably, vacant land is NOT taxed at the top of the range, unlike a pure Georgist vacant-land-penalty design — it sits at the low end of the residential band).
transition_mechanism: A capped-percentage-increase phase-in, distinct from anything currently on the wiki's transition-objection pages: the Bill proposes that if a property's new land-value-based tax exceeds its current bill, the increase is capped at 20% per year until the new benchmark is reached (worked example given in the article: ₹10,000 → ₹12,000 → ₹14,400 → ₹17,280 → ₹20,000 over four years to reach a ₹20,000 benchmark). Where the new land-value assessment would produce a LOWER tax than the current bill, the article states the existing (higher) amount is retained as the benchmark rather than an immediate cut — i.e., the transition is asymmetric, capping increases but not immediately passing through decreases either.
no_water_or_power_mechanism_clarified: IMPORTANT PRECISION for T1: the 'no water or power' enforcement is NOT a property-tax-delinquency tool — it is a building-code/occupancy-certificate enforcement tool, legally separate from the tax reform. Direct quote: 'Under Section 167, buildings without an occupancy certificate would not be provided electricity, drinking water or sewerage connections.' This applies to unauthorized/uncertified construction, alongside penalties of 100%-300% of a building's property tax for illegal construction (Section 164, with a 15-day notice-to-cure period before the municipal commissioner can order demolition and recover costs via the tax bill) and the power to seal a building without prior notice where public safety is at issue (Section 165). The headline conflates two distinct CURE provisions (the tax-base reform and the illegal-construction enforcement regime) under one 'what CURE means' framing; a wiki page should separate them clearly.
existing_wiki_coverage: India property-tax coverage on the wiki is thin, as flagged: research/india-mohua-value-capture-framework.md (India's Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs value-capture framework — likely the closest existing thematic relative, worth checking for direct overlap before drafting) and research/sampat-india-rentier-growth-infrastructure.md are the closest existing pieces; events/2024-india-mineral-royalty-tax-ruling.md is India content but about mining royalty, not property tax. No existing page covers Telangana, Hyderabad, GHMC, or any Indian municipal property-tax reform specifically — this would be the wiki's first.
uncertainties: 1. This is a BILL, not enacted law — as of publication (Sep 12) it had only been introduced, following a July 4-24 public-feedback period in which property tax was 'the biggest concern, with 2,465 submissions opposing an increase' — a T1 should track whether it passes before writing this up as settled policy rather than a live proposal. 2. I did not fetch the primary Bill text (43 chapters, 319 sections per the article) — all section numbers and figures above are as reported by NewsMeter, a regional Indian news outlet, not independently verified against Telangana government sources. 3. 'Annual rental value' (ARV) is itself a distinct valuation method from 'capital value' (used in, e.g., much of India including some other cities) — I have not verified what Hyderabad's CURRENT system technically is beyond the article's characterization as 'rental value-based,' which a T1 with India property-tax expertise should sanity-check. 4. The relationship between this Bill's Property Identity Code system and its land-value tax base (whether land values will be assessed via a stated methodology, guideline/circle rates, or something else) is not described in this article and would need a second source.

title: Op-Ed: Libya's economy — when policy makes rent-seeking more profitable than production (Libya Herald, Husni Bey, published 2026-08-20)
what_was_fetched: Full op-ed text obtained via r.jina.ai reader proxy (HTTP 200, complete extraction — the whole piece, clearly bounded by opening/closing quote marks in the source) and confirmed accessible directly via curl (HTTP 200, page title confirms author and framing). Full-text A-grade fetch of the actual op-ed as published (a secondary editorial framing paragraph precedes it, explicitly labeling it 'this opinion piece' by 'leading Libyan businessman Husni Bey').
verdict: REJECT — confirms the default expectation. This is a pure argumentative op-ed by a non-economist businessman, in a small English-language Libyan outlet, containing specific-sounding figures that are the author's own unsourced estimates rather than citable data points, on a subject (currency-arbitrage and fuel-subsidy rent-seeking) that is at best at the far edge of the wiki's rent-gradient scope and has zero existing wiki infrastructure (no Libya page, no DUP/rent-seeking-currency page) to attach it to.
claim_grade: D — advocacy source (a businessman's opinion piece), explicitly labeled as such by the outlet's own framing paragraph. Under EDITORIAL's source-quality hierarchy this sits at tier 6, 'only to represent that advocate's own position' — and there is no existing wiki position on Libya's currency/subsidy system for it to represent one side of.
does_it_contain_verifiable_specifics: Yes, more than a typical op-ed — this is its main point of interest even in rejection. Named/quantified claims include: Libya earns '93%' of public revenue from oil/gas in foreign currency (mostly USD) but spends '100%' domestically in dinars; the official exchange rate is cited as 'around LYD 6.35 to the dollar'; a personal foreign-exchange allowance of up to $2,000 per citizen for '~4 million' eligible Libyans, implying theoretical demand of 'up to $8 billion'; a parallel-market premium of '30% or more'; the 2016-2019 official/parallel exchange-rate gap 'over 1000%,' explicitly naming then-Central-Bank-of-Libya-Governor Saddik El-Kabir as the period's key official; and an estimate that preferential-FX-access rent 'could amount to tens of billions of dinars annually, potentially approaching LYD 48 billion.' The op-ed also names a specific reform direction: shifting fuel subsidies 'from subsidising the commodity price to supporting the citizen directly in cash' — i.e., replacing an in-kind/price subsidy with a cash transfer, which is conceptually adjacent to (though not framed as) a rent-dividend mechanism.
why_reject_despite_specifics: None of these figures carry a citation within the op-ed itself — no CBL report, IMF Article IV consultation, or World Bank data is named as the source for the 93% revenue-currency split, the LYD 48 billion rent estimate, or the 1000% exchange-gap claim. They read as the author's own back-of-envelope calculations (he states the $8 billion figure is 'theoretical demand generated by that policy alone,' explicitly a derived estimate, not a reported fact). Husni Bey is described only as a 'leading Libyan businessman' — not an economist, central banker, or academic — so this is a practitioner's informed opinion, not a source with institutional standing to cite for the figures themselves. The wiki has zero existing Libya coverage (confirmed by repo grep: no places/libya.md, no research or objections pages mentioning Libya) and no dedicated page on currency-arbitrage rent-seeking or dual-exchange-rate rents as a DUP (directly-unproductive-profit-seeking) case study, so there is no natural, lower-bar home (e.g., an existing page's 'further reading' list) to slot a D-grade citation into.
existing_wiki_coverage: None. No Libya page, no dual-exchange-rate or currency-arbitrage rent-seeking page exists anywhere on the wiki.
uncertainties: 1. If T1 independently decides Libya's currency/subsidy rent-seeking situation is worth a page on its own merits (it is a clean, textbook rent-seeking case study conceptually, fitting the wiki's stated 'all rents' scope-expansion mission), the RIGHT sourcing path is to go around this op-ed to primary data — an IMF Libya Article IV consultation (IMF publishes these regularly and they would independently confirm or correct the 93%/6.35/1000%-gap figures), CBL's own published exchange-rate data, or World Bank Libya Economic Monitor reports — not to cite Husni Bey's estimates as the numbers themselves. 2. I have not attempted to verify any of the op-ed's figures against outside sources in this session; I flag them only as 'specific and checkable in principle,' not as verified. 3. The subsidy-to-cash-transfer proposal is the one piece of this op-ed with the closest conceptual tie to the wiki's existing citizen's-dividend/UBI-scope-rule content (EDITORIAL's UBI rule requires a rent/commons-funding tie) — but a fuel subsidy reform funded by ending an existing subsidy, not by a rent-capture instrument, does not obviously clear that bar either; a T1 more expert in the UBI scope rule's edges should make that call, not this brief.

Did NOT fetch the primary legislative text (Act No. 615 of 30 June 2026) from Retsinformation.dk or another Danish government source.
verdict: ENRICH places/denmark.md 'Contemporary Status' section — genuinely new, dated legislative detail (2026 Act) that the current, fairly thin 'Contemporary Status' paragraph does not have; bears partly, not solely, on the land/grundskyld component.
claim_grade: B — full text of a specific, section-cited law-firm summary (the precision of the section numbers — 87c, 88b, 33a, 83c, 83d, 84b, new 6(2) — suggests direct, competent familiarity with the actual statute), but this is marketing content from the firm representing (unstated) clients in this practice area, not an independent or peer-reviewed source, and I did not cross-check the section numbers or effective dates against the primary Act text myself. Treat as reliable for what the firm says the law does, not as neutral analysis of its significance.
what_changed_and_when: Act No. 615 of 30 June 2026, amending the Danish Property Assessment Act (Ejendomsvurderingsloven), the Property Tax Act (Ejendomsskatteloven) and other acts, entered into force 1 July 2026. Four distinct changes: (1) EXTENDS a simplified 'indexed' valuation methodology (mechanically indexing a prior valuation to current price levels rather than doing a full fresh individual assessment) from its prior 2024-2025 use to also cover the 2026 and 2027 valuation years — residential properties (valued in even years) get their 2026 valuation by indexing the 2022 valuation (or a later reassessment) forward; properties valued in odd years get their 2027 valuation similarly indexed from ~2023. Indexed valuations themselves are NOT subject to administrative appeal, though the underlying valuation they're indexed FROM remains appealable. (2) Creates a NEW unified statutory property category, from the 1 January 2027 valuation date, for 'agricultural, forest and nature' properties in rural zones — covering land used for nature, biodiversity, wetlands, fallow land, etc., giving them the more favorable valuation/tax treatment already applied to farm/forest land; new section 33a lets an owner request a binding advance ruling on how a change to their property affects its categorization; new section 83d gives an 'advance categorisation' procedure (with the Danish Tax Agency issuing early decisions ahead of the ordinary 2027 valuation) plus a new 'transitional scheme' (83c) letting a property continue to be treated as residential until ownership changes — note: once opted into, the transitional-scheme choice CANNOT be reversed; a new 'preliminary tax base' (84b) is assigned in the interim, used to assess property value tax, LAND TAX (this is the direct hit on the grundskyld question), and coverage charges until the first ordinary valuation issues (Tax Agency expects to start processing in H2 2026, with decisions in Q1 2027). (3) A NEW, narrow land-tax relief: new section 6(2) of the Property Tax Act lets an owner apply to their municipal council for exemption from any INCREASE IN LAND TAX that would otherwise result from subdividing a property to create new owner-occupied residential units in an existing building's unused loft/attic space or new added storeys — i.e., a targeted grundskyld relief specifically to encourage adding housing units within existing building envelopes ('roof apartment' densification), so the land tax doesn't rise just because the parcel is subdivided into more titled units. (4) Extends the deadline to request reassessment of the underlying 2022 and 2023 valuations (the base years for the indexed 2026/2027 valuations) by two years each — 2022 valuations: now appealable to 1 May 2030 (was 2028); 2023 valuations: to 1 May 2031 (was 2029) — this extension applies equally to the tax authorities' own right to reassess.
does_it_bear_on_land_value_specifically: Partly, genuinely, not just buildings/commercial. The clearest direct hit is item (3) above — a new grundskyld-specific (land tax) relief provision, and item (2)'s 'preliminary tax base... used to assess... land tax' language. But the largest single change — item (1), the indexed-valuation-methodology extension — applies to the OVERALL property valuation system (which in Denmark separately assesses land value for grundskyld purposes and total property value for property-value tax / ejendomsværdiskat), so it affects land valuations too, but is not a land-specific policy change; it's a valuation-METHOD change (indexing vs. full reassessment) that applies across the board. The rural-property recategorization (item 2) is about which VALUATION REGIME a rural parcel falls under (favorable ag/forest treatment vs. ordinary residential/commercial), which indirectly determines the land-tax base for those specific properties but isn't a rate or base change to grundskyld generally.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/denmark.md (last_reviewed 2026-07-18) covers grundskyld's history (1903-1933 legislative chronology), the Justice Party's 1957-1960 high-water mark, and — its strongest current content — the 2007 municipal-boundary-reform capitalization debate (DORS finding full capitalization vs. Nielsson/Wroblewski/Yding finding a precise zero effect). Its 'Contemporary Status' section is currently generic and thin: 'the share of Danish local government revenue coming from the grundskyld has varied... debates... frequently revisit the question of how to apportion the tax between land and building values... remains a live element of Danish fiscal policy' — no specific 2026 legislative content at all. This Act No. 615 material would be the first concrete, dated update to that section since the page was last reviewed.
uncertainties: 1. I did not fetch or verify the primary Act No. 615 text from Retsinformation.dk (Denmark's official legal-information portal) — all section numbers and effective dates above are as stated by the law firm, not independently cross-checked. Given how specific and technical the citations are (exact section numbers, exact deadline dates), I'd rate the risk of outright fabrication as low, but a T1 should still verify before publishing exact dates/section numbers as wiki facts. 2. This is fundamentally administrative/procedural legislation (valuation methodology, appeal deadlines, a narrow densification relief) rather than a rate change, base change, or ideological shift in Denmark's land-tax policy — it does not bear on the wiki's live capitalization-evidence debate (DORS vs. Nielsson et al.) at all, and a T1 should not oversell its significance; it's a solid, dateable 'contemporary status' update, not a new data point for the incidence debate. 3. I don't know whether 'coverage charges' (dækningsafgift — the commercial-property surcharge separate from grundskyld) is materially affected here beyond being listed alongside land tax and property-value tax in the 84b 'preliminary tax base' language; the article doesn't elaborate coverage-charge-specific detail. 4. The firm's practice-area self-interest (advising clients on exactly these changes) means the piece may selectively emphasize provisions that create billable advisory work (the appeal-deadline extensions, the binding-ruling procedure) — worth keeping in mind when weighting which parts of this to feature on the wiki page.
